questions.q: Consider the function $f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}sin \left(x - 4\right). \tan^{-1} \left(\dfrac{1}{x - 4}\right)$& x \ne 4 \\ 0 & x = 4\end{cases},\right$ then$
options: $f ( x )$ is continuous and differentiable at $x = 4$
$f  \left(x\right)$ is continuous but non differentiable at $x = 4$
$f  \left(x\right)$ is discontinuous and non differentiable at $x = 4$
questions.solution:
Let us shift the graph of $f\left(x\right)$ in the direction of the negative $x -$axis by $4$ units
& let $g\left(x\right) = f\left(x + 4\right)$
$∵ g\left(x\right)$ at $x = 0$ will have the same behaviour as of $f\left(x\right)$ at $x = 4$
$g\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}sin ⁡ x . {tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) \\ 0\end{array}\begin{array}{ll}x \ne 0 \\ x = 0\end{array}\right$
Continuity at $x = 0$,
$\lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}g\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}sin ⁡ x . {tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = 0 \times \left(- \pi / 2\right) = 0$
$\lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}g\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}sinx . {tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = 0 \times \left(\pi / 2\right) = 0$
$∴ \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}g\left(x\right) = g\left(0\right) ∴ g\left(x\right)$ is continuous at $x = 0$
$⇒ f\left(x\right)$ is continuous at $x = 4$
Differentiability at $x = 0$
${g}^{'}\left({0}^{-}\right) = \lim_{\text{h} \to {0}^{+}}\dfrac{\text{g}\left(0 - \text{h}\right) - \text{g}\left(0\right)}{- \text{h}} = \lim_{\text{h} \to {0}^{+}}\dfrac{\text{sin}\left(- \text{h}\right){\text{tan}}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{- 1}{\text{h}}\right) - 0}{- \text{h}}$
$⇒ \lim_{h \to {0}^{+}} - \left(\dfrac{sinh}{h}\right)ta{n}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{h}\right) = - 1 . \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{- \pi}{2}$
${g}^{'}\left({0}^{+}\right) = \lim_{\text{h} \to {0}^{+}}\dfrac{\text{g}\left(0 + \text{h}\right) - \text{g}\left(0\right)}{\text{h}} = \lim_{\text{h} \to {0}^{+}}\dfrac{\text{sin h} . {\text{tan}}^{- 1}\dfrac{1}{\text{h}} - 0}{\text{h}}$
$⇒ \lim_{h \to {0}^{+}}\left(\dfrac{sinh}{h}\right)ta{n}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{h}\right) = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$
Clearly, ${g}^{'}\left({0}^{-}\right) \ne {g}^{'}\left({0}^{+}\right)$
$∴ g\left(x\right)$ is non-differentiable at $x = 0$
$⇒ f\left(x\right)$ is non-differentiable at $x = 4$

The given function is clearly continuous at all points except possibly at $x = \pm 1 .$
For $f\left(x\right)$ to be continuous at $x = 1,$ we must have
$\lim_{x \to {1}^{-}}f\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to {1}^{+}}f\left(x\right) = f\left(1\right)$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta = 1$ … $\left(1\right)$
Now, for $f\left(x\right)$ to be differentiable at $x = 1,$ we must have
$\lim_{x \to {1}^{-}}\dfrac{f\left(x\right) - f\left(1\right)}{x - 1} = \lim_{x \to {1}^{+}}\dfrac{f\left(x\right) - f\left(1\right)}{x - 1}$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to {1}^{-}}\dfrac{\alpha{x}^{2} - \alpha}{x - 1} = \lim_{x \to {1}^{+}}\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{{x}^{2}} - 1}{x - 1}$
$⇒ \lim_{x \to {1}^{-}}\alpha\left(x + 1\right) = \lim_{x \to {1}^{+}}\dfrac{- 2}{{x}^{3}} ⇒ 2\alpha = - 2$
$⇒ \alpha = - 1$
Putting $\alpha = - 1$ in $\left(1\right),$ we get $\beta = 2$
